Foundations 1

Salesforce cases to email and Jira issues

Foundational 90 minutes Lab 1 of 6
Introduction
  1. Monday · 9:02 AM
    Dana opens her laptop. Forty-seven new Salesforce cases overnight.
    01
  2. 9:47 AM
    She copies each case into Jira by hand. Three slip through the cracks. The team only notices on Tuesday.
    02
  3. 10:15 AM
    Dana decides today is the day a recipe takes the typing job.
    03

In this lab, you'll act as automation engineer for Anitech — building the recipe that handles Dana's case sync automatically, so she never copies another row by hand.

DR
Dana Reyes
Support Lead · Anitech

Spends the first two hours of every shift copying Salesforce cases into Jira by hand.

The question

How do you stop hand-copying Salesforce cases without dropping any?

You'll learn how to

  • Configure a Salesforce trigger and an Email by Workato action with mapped datapills
  • Clone and adapt a recipe for an enhanced use case
  • Write a formula to transform a datapill in place
  • Build conditional logic to deduplicate Jira issues
  • Wrap critical steps with error handling and surface failures over email
  • Customize the job report so business context is visible at a glance

What you'll need

  • Access to the training workspace and two preconfigured connections (Salesforce, Jira)
  • A pre-provisioned student project that contains a Connections folder and a Recipes folder
Phase 1

Notice the cases

Can the recipe see what Dana sees?

Pattern

Notifier

The Notifier is the simplest iPaaS shape: watch one system for an event, tell a person about it, and stop. The trigger watches Salesforce for new cases, and the email is the entire response. The plumbing is mechanical; the actual design decision is in deciding what's worth telling someone.

1.1

Create the lab folder

A Workato project is your isolated workspace — your training project is separate from anyone else's. Folders are how you stay tidy inside it as recipes, connections, and any other assets accumulate. One folder for this lab keeps the lab's assets together.

Overview

Create a folder called Foundations 1 inside your student project's Recipes folder. Both recipes for this lab — and any other assets you add later — will live here.

Apply these values

New folder nameFoundations 1
Detailed steps 5 steps

Everything you build in this lab lives inside one folder so it's easy to find. When it comes time to build production recipes, folders help manage recipes, connections, and other assets so they're easy to find, track, and develop.

  • In the left navigation, choose Projects and open your assigned student project.

  • Open the Recipes folder.

  • Choose Create > Folder in the top-right corner.

  • Name the new folder Foundations 1 and confirm.

  • Open the new folder. It will be empty, as expected.

Verify that Foundations 1 appears as a folder inside Recipes and that clicking it opens an empty folder.

1.2

Configure the Salesforce trigger

Dana spends the first two hours of every shift watching Salesforce for new cases. The recipe takes over that watching — but only if it can see what she sees. That's the trigger's job.

Overview

Create a recipe in Foundations 1, named [REC] - 001 - Salesforce Case to Email Notification. Set its trigger to Salesforce → New records on the Cases object. Use 01/01/2025 for When first started so the first poll has historical cases to find. Save the recipe but don't start it yet.

AppSalesforce (WOW_US)
Trigger eventNew records
ConnectionSalesforce Connection — Your attendee name
ObjectCases
When first started01/01/2025
Detailed steps 9 steps

You'll point the trigger at the Cases object using the preconfigured Salesforce connection and a start date old enough to find real data.

  • In the top-right corner, choose Create > Recipe.

  • Name the recipe [REC] - 001 - Salesforce Case to Email Notification and set the location to Foundations 1.

  • In the recipe editor, choose Pick a starting point, then Trigger from an app.

  • Click the trigger step, search for Salesforce (WOW_US) in the configuration panel, and select it.

  • Save the recipe.

Verify that the trigger step shows a green check, the data drawer lists Salesforce Case datapills (Case Number, Subject, Status, Priority, Description), and the recipe saved without warnings.

1.3

Map datapills into an Email by Workato send

Noticing a case is useless if no one hears about it. An email is the lightest way for Dana to be notified. In this task, we'll ensure the cases get surfaced into Dana's inbox. In Phase 2, you'll build on this recipe to track cases in Jira.

Overview

Add an Email by Workato → Send email action under the trigger. Build the Subject and Message by clicking each Case datapill into place. Run Test recipe to send one email and confirm the wiring. Don't start the recipe yet.

Heads up

Don't type in the field names. The datapills bind the case data into subsequent actions; typed text is just a label.

The recipe needs to take the Salesforce fields it learned about and drop them into an email. Instead of typed names, you'll insert real data from the Recipe data menu.

Phase 2

Don't make duplicates

How does the recipe know if it's already handled this case?

Pattern

App-to-app sync (point-to-point)

App-to-app sync is the second-most-common iPaaS shape: two systems of record kept in agreement. The defining problem is idempotency — running the recipe ten times must produce the same end state as running it once. That's why the next few tasks are about not making duplicates.

2.1

Clone the recipe and switch the trigger

Emails work for one person, but the rest of the team can't see them, and they fall out of date the moment Dana reads them. What the team needs is a Jira board to track the work. Clone the working recipe and evolve the copy toward Jira.

Overview

Clone the working recipe, rename the clone to [REC] - 002 - New/Updated Salesforce Cases to Jira Issues, and keep it in Foundations 1. Open the clone's trigger and switch its event from New records to New/Updated records. This switch sets up the deduplication work in the next tasks. Leave everything else alone for now.

Apply these values
FieldValue
Source recipe[REC] - 001 - Salesforce Case to Email Notification
Cloned recipe name[REC] - 002 - New/Updated Salesforce Cases to Jira Issues
New trigger eventNew/Updated records
Detailed steps 6 steps

Switching the trigger from "New records" to "New/Updated records" sets up the deduplication scenario in the next task: updates need to find the existing Jira issue, not create a new one each time.

  • Open the recipe [REC] - 001 - Salesforce Case to Email Notification.

  • From the recipe action menu, choose Clone.

  • Rename the cloned recipe to [REC] - 002 - New/Updated Salesforce Cases to Jira Issues and confirm the clone is saved in your Foundations 1 folder.

  • Open the cloned recipe, switch it into edit mode, and click the trigger step.

  • Change the trigger event from New records to New/Updated records.

  • Save the recipe.

Verify that both recipes exist in the Foundations 1 folder, the cloned recipe's trigger reads New/Updated records, and the Email by Workato action from the original is still wired up.

2.2

Upcase the priority into the subject with a formula

The cloned recipe still sends the same plain-fields email as recipe 001. A support channel gets dozens of these a day; a Priority label buried mid-message doesn't help anyone triage faster. Put it where it can't be missed: the subject line, in capitals.

Overview

On the cloned recipe's Email by Workato step, switch Subject to Formula mode, then open Ask AIRO and describe the transform in plain English: put the upcased Salesforce Priority in front of the subject. Read the formula AIRO drafts, apply it, and check that the subject starts with the priority in capitals, such as HIGH, followed by the case subject.

Apply these values
FieldValue
Subject field modeFormula
AIRO promptAdd the Salesforce priority from step 1 to the beginning of the subject field of step 2, then upcase the priority label.
Expected resultA formula that upcases PriorityStep 1 and places it before SubjectStep 1. The exact formula AIRO writes can differ.
Detailed steps 7 steps

This is the first time a datapill gets transformed instead of inserted as-is. AIRO drafts the formula from a plain-English description, but AI can miss the mark, and its output can change from one run to the next. Reading the formula it returns, and correcting it if needed, is what builds the transform-syntax literacy.

  • Open the cloned recipe and click the Email by Workato action's Subject field.

  • Switch the field from Text to Formula using the toggle.

  • In the toolbar at the bottom of the canvas, choose Ask AIRO to open the chat panel.

  • Ask AIRO: Add the Salesforce priority from step 1 to the beginning of the subject field of step 2, then upcase the priority label.

  • Wait for AIRO to finish. Choose View update details to see what it changed, then choose Apply updates. The change does not reach the recipe until you apply it.

  • Open the Subject field and read the formula AIRO wrote. It should upcase the Priority datapill and place it ahead of the Subject datapill. AI can make mistakes: if the formula doesn't do that, edit it by hand or ask AIRO again.

  • Save the recipe and run Test recipe to confirm the subject line now leads with the upcased priority.

Verify that the Subject field is in Formula mode, AIRO's update is applied, and a test run produces a subject line starting with the case's priority in capital letters, followed by the original subject text.

2.3

Search Jira for an existing issue

The recipe will run every few minutes. If it created an issue on every run, each update to a case would add another duplicate to the team's Jira board. Before writing anything, the recipe has to ask: have I seen this case before?

Overview

Add a Jira (WOW_US) → Search Issues step between the trigger and the Email by Workato action in recipe 2. Write the JQL (Jira Query Language) to find the Case Number in the issue's Labels field, which is how the recipe recognizes a case it has seen. The output drawer then offers a List size datapill; the next two tasks branch on it.

Apply these values
FieldValue
AppJira (WOW_US)
ActionSearch Issues
ConnectionJira Connection — Your name
JQL querylabels = " + Case Number datapill (Step 1) + "

Dedup contract: the search step returns a list. The next If/Else if reads the list size and routes to Create (size = 0) or Update (size = 1). If the size is greater than 1, neither branch gets called. That gap is deliberate; Task 2.5 asks you to think it through.

Detailed steps 6 steps

The Search Issues action with a JQL query keyed off the Salesforce Case Number is how the recipe asks "does this case already have a Jira issue?". The result is a list, and the list's size is what the next condition will branch on.

  • In the cloned recipe, click the + below the trigger and choose Action in an app.

  • Search for Jira (WOW_US) and select it.

  • Choose the action Search Issues.

  • Select the preconfigured connection Jira Connection - <your name>.

  • Click into the JQL query field. Type labels = ", insert the Case Number datapill from Step 1, then type the closing ".

  • Save the step.

Verify that Step 2's data drawer offers an Issues list with a List size datapill underneath it, and a test run returns either zero or one matching issue without throwing a JQL syntax error.

2.4

Branch — create a new Jira issue when none exists

When the search answers "no match," Jira has nothing about this Case yet. Create a fresh issue with the Case fields mapped over. Stash the Case Number in Labels; that's the key the next re-run will search by when this same case updates.

Overview

Under the Search step, add an If condition reading Step 2 List size equals 0. Nest a Jira → Create Issue action inside it. Map the Case fields, set Labels to the Case Number, and build a formula so every Summary starts with the Case Number prefix, such as [CASE-5003] Login fails on mobile.

Key insight

One question, three answers — but only two are handled

The Search step turned "have I seen this Case?" into a number. Zero matches means new: create the issue. Exactly one match means seen before: update it in the next task. More than one match is a third answer the If/Else if doesn't route anywhere; Task 2.5 asks you to sit with this gap before deciding what to do about it.

Apply these values
FieldValue
ConditionList sizeStep 2 equals 0
If branch action — AppJira (WOW_US)
If branch actionCreate issue
ProjectSUP — your assigned Support project
SummaryFormula: "[CASE-" + Case NumberStep 1 + "] " + SubjectStep 1
DescriptionDescriptionStep 1
LabelsCase NumberStep 1
Issue prioritypriority.name → PriorityStep 1
Detailed steps 9 steps

An If condition reads the search result's list size: when the size is zero — nothing came back — the recipe creates a fresh Jira issue from the Case fields and tags it with the Case Number in Labels, so the next run can find it. The Priority is selected as priority.name; the Salesforce value must match one of Jira's priority names, or the create step rejects it.

  • Below Step 2 (Search Issues), click the + and choose If Condition.

  • Configure the condition: Data field = List size (from Step 2 output), Condition = equals, Value = 0. This branch runs when the search found nothing — a brand-new Case.

  • Inside the If block, click +, choose Action in an app, select Jira (WOW_US), choose Create issue, and pick your Jira connection.

  • Set Project to your assigned Support project (SUP).

  • Click into the Summary field and switch it to Formula mode with the fx toggle.

  • Build the formula in two pasted pieces and two datapills. Paste "[CASE-" + into the field, insert the Case Number datapill from Step 1, paste + "] " + , then insert the Subject datapill from Step 1. The result reads "[CASE-" + Case Number + "] " + Subject. Paste the text; don't type it. The editor adds a closing ] and quote as you type [ and ", so typing key by key leaves a stray ].

  • Description ← Description (Step 1).

  • For Issue priority, open the dropdown, choose Priority name, and insert the Priority datapill from Step 1.

  • Labels ← Case Number (Step 1) — this is the dedup tag the Search step queries. Save the step.

Verify that the If condition reads Step 2 List size equals 0, the nested Create Issue step has datapills in Project, Summary (a formula), Description, Labels, and Issue priority, and a dry-run with a brand-new Case ID creates a Jira issue whose title starts with [CASE-…] and whose Labels contains the Case Number.

2.5

Else-if branch — update the existing Jira issue

The search found a match: Jira already has an issue for this Case. But Cases evolve: priority shifts, descriptions sharpen, status moves. If the recipe doesn't update the Jira row to match, the team triages stale data.

Overview

Beside the If, add an Else if with the List size equals 1 predicate. Inside it, add Jira → Update Issue with the same field mapping as Create, plus Issue ID. Run the recipe twice against the same Case: first it creates the issue, then it updates it. No duplicate.

Note

What if Search Issues finds more than one?

We're using List size equals 1 on purpose: it only fires when there's exactly one match to update. Two Cases already went through: one hit If (created), one now hits Else if (updates). Neither branch fires if a Case ever comes back with two or more matching Jira issues; right now the recipe would silently do nothing for that record. Before you move on: how would you even end up with two matching issues for one Case? And once you're there, what should the recipe do: pick one, flag it, something else?

Apply these values
FieldValue
BranchElse if
ConditionList size (Step 2) equals 1
Action — AppJira (WOW_US)
ActionUpdate issue
Issue ID or KeyIDStep 2
SummaryFormula: "[CASE-" + Case NumberStep 1 + "] " + SubjectStep 1
DescriptionDescriptionStep 1
Issue prioritypriority.name → PriorityStep 1
Detailed steps 7 steps

The other side of dedup. When Search Issues found exactly one match, the recipe updates that issue instead of creating a duplicate. Same field mapping as Create, plus the Issue ID coming back from Step 2: that's the key that tells Jira which row to write to. equals 1 is deliberate, not greater than 0: the recipe should only update when it's certain which issue it's updating.

  • Below the If block, click + and choose Else If Condition.

  • Configure the condition: Data field = List size (Step 2), Condition = equals, Value = 1.

  • Inside the Else If block, click + and choose Action in an app.

  • Select Jira (WOW_US) and choose Update issue.

  • Map Issue ID or Key ← ID datapill from Step 2 (Search issues, under Issues), not from the trigger and not from Step 4. The data drawer opens on Step 4, Create issue, whose ID pill looks the same but belongs to the other branch. Switch to Step 2 before you pick the pill.

  • Map Summary, Description, and Issue priority the same way as Task 2.4, including the Summary formula. That keeps the [CASE-…] prefix on the title after an update.

  • Save the recipe.

Verify that running the recipe twice against the same Case creates the Jira issue on the first run and updates it (no duplicate) on the second, and that a Case whose search returns two or more matches hits neither branch, so the recipe leaves it alone rather than guessing.

Phase 3

Survive failure

When the recipe breaks, what saves Dana from finding out by surprise?

Pattern

Operational hardening

Operational hardening is what turns a working integration into one a team can leave alone: error handling, alerting, and a readable job report. Most teams add this late, after the integration is proven. The next two tasks are the foundational hardening moves: catch failures, surface case context in the Jobs view.

3.1

Wrap the critical path with error handling

A recipe that fails silently at 3 AM is worse than one that doesn't run. The team assumes the sync is fine while Cases pile up. Networks die, APIs change, fields rename. Wrap the critical path so failures surface as an email rather than as silence.

Overview

Wrap the Search, If, and Else if steps in a Monitor block. On the block's Error found? Yes branch, add Email by Workato → Send email to notify someone who can act when any wrapped step throws, with the recipe name and error message. Leave the notification email from recipe 001 outside the Monitor; only the Jira logic needs the safety net.

Apply these values
FieldValue
Wrapper stepHandle errors
Wrapped stepsSearch Issues, If, Else if, and their nested actions
Error-notify action — AppEmail by Workato
Error-notify actionSend email
ToYour own email address
Subject[ERROR] + Subject (Step 1)
MessageInclude error details, Case Number, Job ID

The Monitor block wraps Search, If, and Else if. The Error found? Yes branch sits below it, holding the Email by Workato action that runs when any wrapped step throws.

Detailed steps 8 steps

The Monitor block catches an error from any wrapped step instead of letting the job fail unseen. The email on its Error found? Yes branch tells a human what broke, and where.

  • In the recipe canvas, click + under the trigger and choose Handle errors.

  • The Handle errors block ships with two empty Select an app and action placeholders: one inside the Monitor block, directly under the Monitor step, and one on the Error found? Yes branch, below Do not retry. Delete the one inside the Monitor block: open its ... menu and choose Delete. Keep the other for step 3.1.5.

  • Drag Search issues into the Monitor block. Hover over the step, grab the dotted handle on its left edge, and drop it on the + directly under the Monitor step. The steps renumber, and Search becomes Step 3. The canvas has no multi-select, so you move the steps in two drags.

  • Drag the IF step into the Monitor block the same way and drop it on the + directly under Search. The IF and Else if blocks and their Create issue and Update issue steps move together, so this is one drag. Leave Send email via Workato from recipe 001 where it is, below the Handle errors block. Only the Jira logic needs the safety net.

  • On the Error found? Yes branch, click the Select an app and action placeholder below Do not retry and choose Email by Workato. Send email is selected for you.

  • Configure To, Subject, and Message to surface the failure context. In the data drawer, the On error output holds the Error message, Error type, and Errored step number pills.

  • Save the recipe.

  • To test the error email, temporarily change the JQL query in the Search issues step to labels = with nothing after the equals sign, then choose Test recipe. When the email arrives, restore the original query and save.

Verify that the recipe canvas shows the dedup steps nested inside the Monitor block, and the deliberately broken JQL query from step 3.1.8 triggers the error email to your inbox.

3.2

Customize the Job Report

The recipe runs all week. On Monday morning Dana opens the Jobs view to spot-check what ran and sees generic rows: Job 12348, Success, a timestamp. To learn what a job did, she has to click in. She wants the Case Number, Priority, and Status right in the job log.

Overview

Customize recipe 2's Jobs view to add three columns: Case Number, Priority, Status. Map each to the corresponding datapill on the trigger step. After this, Dana can skim a week of runs and see what each case was about without clicking into a single row.

Apply these values
FieldValue
SectionJobs
ActionCustomize Job Table
Columns to addCase Number, Priority, Status
Mapping sourceRecipe data → Step 1 (Salesforce New/Updated records) datapills
Detailed steps 6 steps

The Jobs view is where the team will scan recent runs. Customize the table to surface the fields that matter.

  • Open the Jobs section of the recipe.

  • Click the three-dot menu and choose Customize Job Table.

  • Add three columns named Case Number, Priority, and Status.

  • For each column, expand Recipe data in the picker, find the datapill from Step 1 (Salesforce New/Updated records), and map it to the column value.

  • Choose Apply changes.

  • Re-run the recipe or trigger an update on a Salesforce Case to populate fresh rows.

Verify that the Jobs table shows three new columns — Case Number, Priority, Status — and a recent job's row displays values straight from the matching Salesforce Case.

Wrap-up

Dana's Monday now starts at 9:02 with an empty Jira-copy queue. The recipe noticed, asked, branched, wrote, and is wired to scream for help if anything goes sideways.

Patterns to carry forward:

  • Clone before you mutate. The original is your fallback while you rebuild the copy.
  • Use datapills. The colored chip is the visual cue that a field is bound to real data, not typed text.
  • Branch on the list size returned by the search. The count tells you exactly which case you're in.
  • Use Monitor blocks to handle errors in critical paths. This beats hoping errors won't happen.

The same shape — trigger, search, branch on list size, wrap with error handling — generalizes to almost any sync-from-system-of-record use case.

Reflect

Dana's queue is clear. Before you ship this recipe, think through the edge cases.

  • Dana asks: "What happens if a case has two matching Jira issues?" What does the recipe do today, and what would you change?
  • A teammate suggests skipping the Monitor block and adding an email step inside the If branch. Why is that worse than the wrapper approach you built?
  • The Summary formula builds the issue title from the Case Number and Subject. If Subject is null on a Case, what does the title look like — and where would you defend against it?
  • Why does Search Issues come before the If/Else if, instead of after? What breaks if you put it after?

Bonus challenges

These are optional, open-ended extensions. There are no click-by-click instructions; reach for what you built.

  • Defend the null priority. The Summary formula assumes the Case fields are set. Add a fallback so a Case with no Priority still creates a clean Jira issue instead of erroring.
  • Pick a winner when two issues match. If Search returns more than one Jira issue for a Case, update the most recently changed one rather than the first. (Hint: sort the results before the branch.)
  • Tell a second channel. Alongside the error email, post failures to a Slack channel so the whole team sees them, not only Dana.
